LONDON, Oct 30 : Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso said Brazilian teenager Estevao would get opportunities this season and dismissed media speculation over a January loan move for the forward ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Manchester United. Spaniard Alonso has come under scrutiny over the 19-year-old's lack of playing time, with Chelsea reeling from a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham Hotspur last week and a League Cup fourth-round exit on penalties at Liverpool on Wednesday. Asked at a press conference on Friday if Estevao could go out on loan, Alonso said: "No discussions about that. "The season is long and there will be moments for everyone. It's a process for the team, for Este, for myself.

"But I'm sure that in the season he'll have his games, his minutes. And we're still early in the season but he'll be there." Estevao has only started two matches in all competitions so far this season and was an unused substitute against Liverpool. "It's no secret that all players want to be on the pitch; they want to be playing," Alonso said. "And when any of them haven't had enough minutes because of my decision, I have to take the responsibility for that, that they are not as happy as they could be." Fifth-placed Chelsea carry a lengthy injury list into Saturday's home match with under-pressure United, who are 16th. Forward Joao Pedro and captain Reece James remain sidelined, while defender Maxence Lacroix is expected to miss a few weeks with a hamstring injury suffered in Wednesday's loss at Anfield. "Max picked up an injury and we expect he is not going to be ready before the (November 9-17) international break," Alonso said. "He will be a few weeks out." There was better news on midfielder Moises Caicedo, who is available despite being forced off against Liverpool with a minor issue. Goalkeeper Emi Martinez, meanwhile, could return before the international break as he recovers from a jaw injury. "We still need to wait until next week, but there's a chance. In case he (Martinez) is ready to play, he will probably need a face mask," Alonso said.

Source: Reuters

ANKARA, Oct 30 : Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt will remain as manager of Fenerbahce until the next international break and will be in the dugout when his old club visit Istanbul in the Champions League next week. The Turkish club said their board had decided to hand Kuyt responsibility for the first team on an interim basis while they search for a permanent head coach. "The committee established by our board will carry out the work to appoint our new head coach, and the process will be accelerated," Fenerbahce said in a statement. Dutchman Kuyt, 46, took over from Ismail Kartal, who resigned following Monday's 2-1 derby defeat by Galatasaray. The former Netherlands international spent six seasons at Liverpool between 2006 and 2012 before joining Fenerbahce, where he won the Turkish league title in 2014.

Source: Reuters

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 30 : While dinosaurs ate a lot of different things, including each other, fruit long seemed to have been absent from their menu. But scientists now have found fossils of a turkey-sized and toothless dinosaur possessing a parrot-like head that exhibited multiple adaptations for a specialized fruit diet. This first-known frugivorous dinosaur, named Infernogallus jamesi, lived about 66 million years ago during the Cretaceous Period at the twilight of the age of dinosaurs and displayed traits on its beak and jaws for mashing soft food like fruit. It is known from fossils unearthed in Montana and North Dakota. The name Infernogallus means "hell chicken," a nod to its bird-like appearance and the fact that its fossils were found in the Hell Creek rock formation, which spans the US states of Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wyoming and has yielded the remains of some of the most famous dinosaurs. It would have eaten fruit and other soft plants in the subtropical coastal floodplain ecosystem it shared with the likes of apex predator Tyrannosaurus, three-horned herbivore Triceratops and tank-like armored plant-eater Ankylosaurus.

Infernogallus was about 5 feet (1.5 meters) long and weighed around 25 pounds (11.3 kg). While the fossils — one nearly complete skeleton and isolated bones from a jaw and palate — did not reveal feathers, the researchers believe Infernogallus was covered in them, based on fossils of close relatives. It belonged to a group called theropods that includes T. rex and all the meat-eating dinosaurs, as well as some that took to eating plants and the entire bird lineage. "This definitely expands the range of lifestyles we thought dinosaurs had, and it shows how adaptable theropods were," said paleontologist Greg Funston of Stony Brook University in New York, lead author of the research published in the journal Nature Communications. Fruits are the reproductive structures of angiosperms, also called flowering plants. Angiosperms first appeared earlier in the Cretaceous, around 130 to 140 million years ago, and subsequently took over landscapes previously dominated by plants called gymnosperms like conifers and ginkgoes. Infernogallus shows that some dinosaurs may have had a close ecological relationship with flowering plants. "It has been proposed before that some groups of dinosaurs ate fruits, but there was never evidence to back it up," said study co-author Thomas Dudgeon, a postdoctoral researcher at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. "The discovery of Infernogallus shows that dinosaur diets were likely far more diverse than we previously thought. Prior to this discovery, there was a bit of a mystery in dinosaur evolution. The evolution of flowering plants introduced a brand-new food source that undoubtedly had consequences for the animals living alongside them," Dudgeon said. The fruit available for Infernogallus may have included various berries as well as drupes, a broad category that today includes types with a central pit like peaches and cherries as well as others like mangoes and olives. THREE KEY FEATURES Infernogallus showed a range of features indicating a frugivorous diet. The three most important, Funston said, were the organization of jaw muscles that powered back-and-forth chewing motions, a mobile joint that enabled the jaw to slide forward, and a series of ridges and grooves on the beak to help mash and shear soft plants like fruits. "We see these features separately in birds and turtles today that eat soft foods, like the fig-eating vulturine parrot or green sea turtles that chew soft sea grass. But no living animal has all three adaptations, showing just how specialized Infernogallus was," Funston said. Infernogallus also shows how adaptable beaks are compared to teeth. "Once you've lost your teeth and developed a beak instead, the range of foods available dramatically increases, including plants, as long as you have some way to digest them," Funston said. Most herbivorous theropods used stomach stones called gastroliths to grind food. But Infernogallus and other members of a lineage called caenagnathids chewed their food instead. Fruit-eating animals play an important role for angiosperms by dispersing seeds. "Mammals and birds would probably also have eaten fruit, but they didn't show the same kinds of specializations for a frugivorous diet that Infernogallus does, so it might have been a less important resource for them. Mammals and birds also were quite small in the Cretaceous, so it's unlikely that they were spreading very large seeds, or that they were spreading them big distances," Funston said. "We know that these big-seeded fruits were proliferating and spreading, and it seems like caenagnathids could have fit this role — although we feel more evidence is needed before drawing that link confidently," Funston said.

Source: Reuters

PARIS, Oct 30 : France's national sports institute INSEP has expelled five teenage basketball players following incidents involving physical violence at its Paris boarding facility, it said on Friday. INSEP had initially suspended 10 players and launched an internal investigation last month after younger players were subjected to acts described as "hazing" by older teammates. "After reviewing the facts and individual responsibilities, five athletes have been permanently expelled from the institution," INSEP said in a statement. "For the other five, the sanctions imposed make it possible to consider their reinstatement at INSEP in the short or medium term, subject to educational measures." Fabien Canu, INSEP's director general, said the decisions taken "make clear that no form of humiliation, harassment, violence or hazing will be tolerated within our institution".

Source: Reuters

Oct 30 : Former England fast bowler James Anderson has said he was shocked when Lancashire chose not to renew his contract, ending a 25-year association with his home county. The 44-year-old, England's leading test wicket taker with 704 victims in 188 matches, retired from international duty in 2024. "I was being told they thought the best way for the team to move forward was without me. I was quite shocked. It was quite brief," Anderson told the BBC Tailenders podcast on Friday. "I wanted to see my career out with Lancs (Lancashire). I don't know if my career is done, we'll have to wait and see, but it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire."

FRANKFURT, Oct 30 : The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on Friday that Russian teams can compete in next year's men's and women's world championships, overturning International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions to exclude them from its competitions. CAS upheld appeals lodged by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the IIHF barring its teams from participating in events during the 2026-27 season. The Lausanne-based court said the IIHF had not presented sufficient evidence to justify its assessment that security concerns required Russia's continued exclusion from its competitions. The first tournament affected by the ruling is the world junior championship in Canada, which begins on December 26.

Other events covered include next year's men's and women's world championships. CAS said the ruling did not address issues such as whether Russian teams should compete under a neutral flag and without national symbols, as athletes from the country have done in other sports. RUSSIA WELCOMES RULING The IIHF has excluded Russia, which has won five IIHF world titles as an independent nation, from most international ice hockey competitions since 2022 following the country's invasion of Ukraine. "Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti. The IIHF said it was disappointed by the outcome. "The IIHF disagrees with this aspect of the ruling and maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions," the federation said. Germany, host of the men's world championship in May, said the ruling had significant implications for the tournament. "Our position remains unchanged: We reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments," German Ice Hockey Federation chairman Frank H. Lutz said. The Czech Ice Hockey Association, whose country is hosting the women's Under-18 world championship in January, said it was "very unpleasantly surprised" by the decision. "The current position of Czech Hockey does not change with the CAS decision," Czech Hockey General Secretary Jan Cerny said. Other European nations including Sweden, Finland and Austria also criticised the ruling. "Our position is that Russia cannot participate in international championships in the current situation," Swedish Ice Hockey Association chairman Anders Larsson said.

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Oct 30 : Alexander Zverev, who spent years waiting for his moment to reach the summit of his sport only for a new golden generation to surge past him, has claimed the honour that long eluded him by climbing to the top of the world rankings. Zverev had long been one of the brightest talents to emerge in the 2010s, but his path, like that of his peers, was largely blocked by the enduring dominance of Roger Federer, Rafa Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray. Despite winning two ATP Finals titles on either side of an Olympic gold medal in 2021, Zverev struggled to make a similar impact at the Grand Slams as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz formed a new roadblock  when the greats began to decline. All that changed this year, however, as Zverev, 29, capitalised on injuries to his major rivals and found another level to claim the French Open and US Open titles.

"It's incredibly special," said Zverev, who will take over from Sinner on Monday and become the 30th man to top the world rankings since they were introduced in 1973. "It's something I've worked towards for years and you have to show great tennis the whole year to be in this position." Zverev will become only the second world number one, after Daniil Medvedev, from the crop of players now largely in their late 20s and early 30s who emerged during the "Big Four" era but never displaced them. ANKLE INJURY The summit had been within Zverev's reach before, but a serious ankle injury at the 2022 French Open derailed his push, and Grand Slam success continued to elude him on his return as Sinner and Alcaraz accumulated 12 majors between them. With Alcaraz's season stalled by a wrist injury and Sinner suffering a knee injury, Zverev's consistency and durability were decisive this year as he triumphed at Roland Garros and Flushing Meadows and reached the Wimbledon final. "I've had a lot of difficult moments in my career: the lost Grand Slam finals, the injury in 2022," Zverev added. "But I always somehow kept believing, kept going. This year I also took the step of changing my game a little and rebuilding it, at 29. The way this season has gone is a dream." Zverev's path to the top has also included turbulence away from the court, with allegations of domestic abuse which he has repeatedly denied. A German court closed a case involving his former partner Brenda Patea after a 2024 settlement without a finding of guilt, and the ATP ended a separate investigation into allegations by Olga Sharypova in 2023, citing insufficient evidence. STAYING POWER Zverev's 3-8 record against top-10 opponents this season may leave room for debate over whether the top ranking makes him the best player, but noted coach Patrick Mouratoglou said staying fit and sustaining excellence were skills in themselves. For Zverev, who has managed Type 1 diabetes since childhood, durability has been a constant issue. "A player is not only performing on court, it's also being healthy, managing your body," Mouratoglou said. "If someone is never injured and others are often injured, the one that's not injured will probably end up having a higher ranking ... staying healthy when you're a professional athlete is a real skill." Zverev said reaching number one late in his career had left him better prepared for the responsibility that accompanies the ranking, both as the face of the sport and the player everyone wants to beat. "The number one position brings a lot with it," said Zverev, Germany's second men's world number one after Boris Becker in 1991. "You have to be a good role model, do a lot of things right and on court that means more than returning and serving well. I still have Carlos and Jannik. Hopefully, I can keep competing with them over the next few years."

HYDERABAD: Indian drug regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical Industries to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, documents reviewed by Reuters showed. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on Aug 20 after a joint federal-state inspection of the facility identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma's move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands. India's drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan. The regulatory agencies' move marks an escalation of the action against Sun Pharma, India's biggest pharmaceutical firm, which will be unable to continue ophthalmic drug production at the Assam factory until it submits a satisfactory compliance report.

Sun Pharma said previously the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver. The regulators sought more information on the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products - liquids used to treat eye conditions - the documents showed. In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, the company said it was withdrawing the products as a "precautionary measure." It remains unclear whether all of the recalled products were contaminated. Sun Pharma did not publicly disclose details of the recall. The company has submitted a compliance report in response to the order, which is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. Sun Pharma did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Assam plant and the recall. The company says on its website it follows a single global quality standard. RECALL COULD INVOLVE HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF BOTTLES Some of the recalled products included Lotepred 1 per cent 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. The eye drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases, according to doctors. It is unclear whether these eye products were exported from India or whether any patients reported any adverse effects.

A man walks past a screen during a press conference announcing Sun Pharma's acquisition of US company, Organon in Mumbai, India, Apr 27, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Francis Mascarenhas)

Reuters found that, based on the product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam state facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 identified brands in the recall notice or included additional brands. The affected batches could translate into hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts, who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly. Ophthalmology contributes about 3 per cent of Sun Pharma's domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of its key areas for the United States. The company reported a drop in second-quarter profit on Friday (Oct 30) weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of US-based Organon. The eye product recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), an independent body of eye specialists, warning that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated. "There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated," Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told Reuters, adding that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops. Sun Pharma did not respond to Reuters' request for comment on the AIOS advisory. The regulators issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on Aug 10, citing the quality management system failures, the documents showed. Dissatisfied with the company's response, the regulators ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility. Indian regulators did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment. The agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall. It is not the first time Sun Pharma's sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the US FDA halted the company's shipments from Gujarat's Halol plant after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.

Source: Reuters/cf

FAST

SINGAPORE: Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance , the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft. WHAT HAPPENED? About US$6.3 billion of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records. Binance said in a statement on X that it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop.

"However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," it added, without elaborating. The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.

Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources. According to US blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorises transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets. The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 8pm GMT (4am, Friday, Singapore time) on Thursday (Oct 29). Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets. An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely. "In layman's terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money," said Joshua Chu, a Hong Kong lawyer who works on crypto cases.  WHO IS BEHIND IT?  Several US blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers. Teng said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers, while North Korea routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea's mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year's attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft. Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.

Related:

Hackers allegedly from North Korea steal US$6.3 billion from Binance in world's biggest crypto heist

WHERE'S THE MONEY? About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture. That doesn't mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers' ability to convert them into cash. TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about US$2.4 billion worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach. "No company issues bitcoin or ether and no company can freeze either one," said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm in Singapore. "The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys." Market participants said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds. "The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers — they essentially get blacklisted," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company. "In reality a lot of the proceeds of hacks ... (can only be laundered) in the first few hours, but after that happens, you have a lot of different players who know those are marked funds ... and they usually sit there for years." WHAT NEXT? The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole US$2.9 billion of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs. The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.

Source: Reuters/rj

Oct 30 : Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, putting a spotlight on how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks. But insurance protection is far from uniform. Coverage depends on how assets are stored, how hackers gain access and the specific terms of the policy. Limited regulation and volatile crypto prices have long made insurers wary of the sector, despite growing demand for protection against digital asset theft and claims against company executives. While both crime and demand for protection have tracked cryptocurrencies' meteoric rise, underwriting such risks remains a niche business offered largely by specialist insurers in the Lloyd's market and in Bermuda.

WHAT IS DIGITAL ASSET INSURANCE? Digital asset insurance is a range of policies designed to protect cryptocurrency exchanges, custodians and other companies operating in the sector against financial losses arising from the theft of digital assets, cyberattacks, technology failures and other business risks. Unlike traditional insurance, these policies are tailored to risks associated with blockchain technology, including the theft or loss of private keys, wallet security breaches, smart contract vulnerabilities and failures in digital asset custody. The global crypto insurance market was valued at $9.37 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $184.98 billion by 2033, according to Data Bridge Market Research. The research firm cited growing institutional adoption of cryptocurrencies and rising incidents of cyberattacks and digital asset theft among the factors driving demand. Coverage can include several types of policies: • Crime insurance for theft, social engineering and scams • Cyber liability for breaches, hacks and regulatory response • Errors and omissions insurance for software bugs, smart contract failures • Directors and officers insurance for lawsuits targeting executives • Technology liability for infrastructure providers HOW ARE LOSSES COVERED? When a crypto exchange suffers a hack, losses can be covered through a combination of insurance payouts, the company's own capital and emergency funds set aside to compensate customers. The extent of insurance coverage depends on the policies held by the exchange, including their limits, deductibles and exclusions. Where losses exceed the insured amount, the company must rely on its own financial resources or other recovery arrangements to meet its obligations. Some exchanges also maintain reserve funds to reimburse customers following security breaches. Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents. As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on its insurance coverage. WHAT CAN PREVENT AN INSURANCE PAYOUT? Exclusions that allow insurers to deny certain claims are common in policies covering digital assets as well as the personal liabilities of directors and officers at cryptocurrency companies. These can limit the scope of protection available to companies and make it harder for them to secure coverage. Common exclusions in these policies include value fluctuations, fraudulent acts by the policyholder and unsecured or negligent key management. DO TRADITIONAL CRIME AND CYBER INSURANCE POLICIES COVER CRYPTO? Most standard crime insurance policies do not cover cryptocurrency losses, as they were originally designed to protect physical property such as cash, securities and precious metals. Traditional cyber liability policies also do not always cover the value of digital assets stolen in a hack. While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds. As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added. HOW DO INSURERS ASSESS CRYPTO THEFT CLAIMS? Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage. They may also assess whether the exchange followed required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals. The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.
